analysis.one_liner: Removes the cap that limits Medicaid drug rebates to a drug's list price.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, was never considered by the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, drug companies selling brand-name drugs to Medicaid must pay rebates to the government, but those rebates can never exceed 100% of the drug's average manufacturer price. That means the government can never recover more through rebates than the drug's list price, no matter how the drug performs. This bill would lift that cap for rebate periods starting in 2020, allowing rebates to exceed the list price and forcing manufacturers to pay more back to Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid programs — financed jointly by states and the federal government — would collect larger rebates from brand-name drug makers, reducing taxpayer costs and potentially lowering drug spending that currently drives up premiums and state budgets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the statutory limit that caps the maximum Medicaid rebate for single-source and innovator multiple-source drugs at 100% of the average manufacturer price for rebate periods beginning January 1, 2020 or later [S2] [S3].
Without the cap, manufacturers could owe rebates exceeding the drug's list price, giving Medicaid — and the federal and state taxpayers who fund it — greater recovery of drug spending [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name (single-source and innovator multiple-source) drug manufacturers would bear larger rebate payments to Medicaid, reducing revenue on drugs sold to the program.

drawbacks.text: Removing the rebate cap could push manufacturers to raise list prices to offset deeper rebates, since Medicaid rebate amounts are calculated from average manufacturer price — a well-known dynamic in the program's rebate formula.
Deeper uncapped rebates could lead manufacturers to raise launch prices or pull products from Medicaid formularies, which could limit access for some enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real distortion: the 100% cap means Medicaid can never recover more through rebates than the drug's list price, letting manufacturers keep the difference on expensive drugs. The main risk is the known price-shift dynamic, where deeper rebates based on list price can encourage higher launch prices — a tradeoff any serious version of this policy would need to manage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Health Subcommittee three weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee that same day, and on January 25, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors over its two-year life [S4].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the 100%-of-price rebate cap remains in place, so Medicaid still cannot recover more in rebates than a drug's list price, and taxpayers and state Medicaid programs continue to absorb the difference.

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lift the Medicaid rebate cap; it received no cosponsors.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 3, 2019 and referred it to its Health Subcommittee; took no further action, never holding a hearing or markup, for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan alignment is visible in the record; the sole sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would end the guarantee that a manufacturer's total Medicaid rebate can never exceed the drug's list price, exposing makers of single-source and innovator multiple-source drugs to rebate liabilities beyond the drug's price. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against taxpayers and Medicaid enrollees, who bear drug costs without it. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: State Medicaid programs and federal taxpayers
industries.note: States and the federal government finance Medicaid; uncapped rebates would reduce what they pay for brand-name drugs for tens of millions of enrollees. [S2]
